subject: Critical Thinking
title: Thinking Like a Fact-Checker: Everyday Habits
description: A 1-minute de-risking session on Thinking Like a Fact-Checker: Everyday Habits.

hook.text: You don't need a journalism degree to check facts.

buildup.text: Habit 1: Check the source before reading the content. Who published this? What's their track record?

discovery.text: Habit 2: Read past the headline. Habit 3: Check the date. Old stories recirculate as if new during crises.

twist.text: Habit 4: reverse-search images to test whether the visual matches the claim.

climax.text: Habit 5: Emotional check. If a story makes you furious, it was designed to. That's your cue to verify, not share.

punchline.text: Five habits. Five seconds each. A lifetime of better information.

quiz.question: Why should you check the date on a news story?
options: Old stories recirculate during crises and are presented as new

details.summary: Thinking like a fact-checker means applying professional verification instincts to everyday information encounters: questioning sources automatically, checking claims laterally, and maintaining a default stance of respectful skepticism.
details.whyItMatters: The habits of professional fact-checkers can be adopted by anyone. These thinking patterns protect against misinformation in every area of life, from health claims to political statements.
takeaways: Professional fact-checker habits are learnable by non-professionals
Default skepticism combined with respect is the ideal stance
Lateral reading is the single most powerful everyday fact-checking technique

faq.question: What is the single most useful habit from professional fact-checkers?
faq.answer: Lateral reading: instead of evaluating a source by reading it deeply, immediately open new tabs to see what other sources say about it. Professional fact-checkers spend less time on the original source and more time checking it against the wider information ecosystem.

faq.question: How do you maintain healthy skepticism without becoming cynical or distrustful?
faq.answer: Skepticism questions claims proportionally to their evidence, not out of blanket distrust. When evidence is strong, accept it provisionally. When it is weak, investigate further. Cynicism rejects everything; skepticism evaluates everything. The difference is in the rigor.
